title: Workplace Violence and Active Shooter Response
standard_title: Workplace violence prevention (General Duty Clause; OSHA and DHS guidance)
summary: Public works crews meet the public every day, often alone, on private property, and sometimes while delivering unwelcome news like a shutoff notice or a road closure. This course defines workplace violence, teaches situational awareness, explains the warning signs to report and how to calm an angry resident or driver, and covers the Run, Hide, Fight response to an active shooter. It also explains how to act when police arrive and how the department supports crews afterward.
objectives: Define workplace violence and identify the four types described by OSHA and NIOSH.
Practice situational awareness in the field by scanning, noting exits, spotting changes from the normal baseline and limiting distractions.
Recognize warning signs of potential violence in coworkers and members of the public and report them through the department's reporting path.
De-escalate a confrontation with an angry resident or driver and disengage safely when it is not working.
Apply the Run, Hide, Fight framework to an active shooter event, including what to do when law enforcement arrives.
Describe the practices the department and each crew use to reduce the risk of violence, such as check-ins for lone workers and radio duress procedures.

sections.heading: What counts as workplace violence
sections.body:
Workplace violence is any act or threat of physical violence, harassment, intimidation or other threatening, disruptive behavior at the work site. That is OSHA's definition. It runs from threats and verbal abuse to physical assault and homicide. A resident who yells that he will 'find out where you live' has committed workplace violence even though he never touched anyone.

OSHA and NIOSH sort it into **four types**, based on who the attacker is:

- **Type 1, criminal intent.** The attacker has no connection to the department and is there to commit a crime, such as stealing copper from a substation or tools from a truck.
- **Type 2, customer or member of the public.** The attacker is someone the department serves: a resident, a ratepayer, a driver in a work zone. For crews who deal with the public all day, this is the type that comes up most.
- **Type 3, worker on worker.** The attacker is a current or former employee.
- **Type 4, personal relationship.** The attacker has a relationship with the victim, usually a current or former partner, and brings that conflict to the job.

sections.heading: Why this training matters
sections.body:
OSHA has no standard written just for workplace violence in public works. The duty comes from **Section 5(a)(1) of the OSH Act**, the General Duty Clause, which requires every employer to provide a workplace free from recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious harm. Violence is one of those hazards. OSHA and the Department of Homeland Security both publish guidance on preventing it, and the department's policy follows that guidance.

Public works crews are more exposed than most workers because of what the job asks:

- You work in public spaces and private yards, often uninvited.
- You shut off water and power, post notices, enforce codes and collect fees. People take that personally.
- Refuse crews hear about missed pickups and damaged carts, sometimes with a fist on the hood.
- Flaggers and street crews close roads and meet drivers who are late and angry.
- You work alone or at night at lift stations, substations, water towers and remote yards.
- Trucks carry tools, copper and sometimes cash, which attracts theft.

The point is not fear. It is to work with your eyes open, know the warning signs, and know exactly what you will do if a situation turns.

sections.heading: Situational awareness
sections.body:
Situational awareness means knowing what is going on around you and what it means for your safety. Most violent events give some warning, and people who are paying attention see it.

Many police and security trainers teach a simple **color code**:

- **White.** Switched off. Headphones in, eyes on a screen. Fine on the couch, never on the job.
- **Yellow.** Relaxed and alert. You notice who is around, where the exits are and what is normal here. This is your working state all day.
- **Orange.** Something caught your attention: a man watching the crew from his porch for twenty minutes, or a coworker who went quiet and red in the face. You focus on it and start a plan.
- **Red.** The threat is real and you act on the plan: leave, call or defend yourself.

Habits that keep you in yellow:

- **Know the baseline.** Every street, lobby and plant has a normal feel. Notice when something is off.
- **Find two exits** in any building, and park so you can pull away without backing up.
- **Put the phone away.** Scrolling turns you white.
- **Trust your gut.** If it feels wrong, step back and call a supervisor. You do not need proof.

Fighter pilots use a loop called **OODA: observe, orient, decide, act**. Take in the scene, work out what it means, pick a response, do it, then look again.

sections.heading: Warning signs, reporting and protective orders
sections.body:
Most people who turn violent at work show signs first. Watch for these in coworkers and in the public:

- Anger that keeps escalating, or outbursts over small things.
- Threats, even 'joking' ones, or talk about weapons and hurting someone.
- Fixation on a grievance: a discipline, a denied claim, a shutoff.
- Intimidation or bullying.
- Substance abuse, or a sudden change in behavior, hygiene or attendance.
- Major life stress such as divorce, money trouble or a death in the family.
- A history of violence.

One sign alone proves nothing, and your job is **not to diagnose** anyone. Your job is to **report** what you saw and heard to your supervisor, the safety office or human resources. If a threat is immediate, call 911 first. Reports go to a **threat assessment team** of human resources, safety, the division manager and, when needed, law enforcement, so no one person decides alone.

**No retaliation.** Reporting a concern in good faith is protected. No one may be disciplined, reassigned or frozen out for raising one.

**Domestic violence follows people to work.** If you have a protective order, or an ex-partner who has threatened you, tell your supervisor or human resources. A photo, a vehicle description and a copy of the order let the front desk, dispatch and gate staff keep that person out, and the department can adjust your schedule or route.

sections.heading: De-escalating an angry resident or driver
sections.body:
Most confrontations end with words, and how you use yours decides which way it goes.

- **Stay calm and lower your voice.** A quiet, steady tone is contagious. So is yelling.
- **Give space.** Stay about two arm lengths away, at an angle rather than square to the person, hands open and visible.
- **Listen first.** Let them finish, then repeat the problem back: 'Your water is off and nobody told you.' People calm down when they feel heard.
- **Do not argue policy.** You did not write the shutoff rule or close the road. Say what you can do, not what you cannot.
- **Offer the supervisor's number** or a card. It gives them a way to win without fighting you.
- **Never block someone's exit**, and never let them block yours. Keep yourself between the person and your truck or the open street.
- **Disengage and leave.** If the person is not calming down, say you will come back another time, walk to the truck and go. Report it before your next stop so the next crew is warned.

Do not touch the person or trade insults, and do not threaten to call the police as a dare. If you need the police, step away and call them.

sections.heading: Active shooter: Run, Hide, Fight
sections.body:
An active shooter is a person actively killing or trying to kill people in a populated area. These events are usually over in minutes, often before police arrive, so the first seconds matter most. The Department of Homeland Security and the FBI teach three options, in order of preference:

1. **Run.** If there is a clear path away from the danger, take it. Leave tools and bags behind. Bring others if they will come; do not wait for anyone who refuses. Keep your hands visible and warn people away from the area. For field crews, **the truck is your escape**: get in, drive away from the sound and do not stop to look. Call 911 once you are safe.
2. **Hide.** If you cannot get out, get out of sight. Pick a room with a door that locks, lock it, turn off the lights and barricade the door with heavy furniture. **Silence your phone completely**, including vibrate. Get behind something solid, spread out, and stay quiet until law enforcement tells you it is clear.
3. **Fight.** Only as a last resort, when your life is in immediate danger. Then **commit completely**; a half effort is worse than none. Use whatever is at hand: a fire extinguisher, a shovel, a chair, your body weight. Work as a group, yell, throw things and go for the weapon arm.

Know **two exits** from every building you work in, including the shop, the plant and city hall, and decide now what you would do in each one. There will be no time to decide then.

sections.heading: When police arrive, and what comes next
sections.body:
Responding officers have one job: **stop the shooter**. They will go past wounded people to do it, and they do not know you from the attacker. Help them:

- Drop anything in your hands. **Empty hands up, fingers spread.**
- No sudden movements. Do not run toward officers or grab them for safety.
- Follow commands exactly, even if they are shouted.
- Do not stop officers to ask for help or directions. Keep moving in the direction they came from.

When you call **911**, give the location, including the building and floor, the number of shooters, what they look like, the kind of weapons and how many people are hurt.

Afterward, go to the **rally point** in your facility's plan and stay there. Supervisors account for every crew member by name and by radio. Do not go back in for anyone or anything, and expect to stay until police release you.

The department will bring in the **employee assistance program** and a critical incident debriefing afterward, and you are expected to use them. Take the yearly active threat walkthrough at your facility seriously. Feet remember what they practiced.

sections.heading: What this means on the job
sections.body:
**Electric Services.** On a disconnect for nonpayment, send two people when the account has a history, keep the truck between you and the door, and leave if the resident escalates; it can be rescheduled. An open gate, a cut lock or a strange vehicle at a substation means back out and call police, not investigate.

**Environmental Services.** Refuse drivers should stay in the cab when a resident runs out to argue, crack the window and offer the customer service number. Operators on night rounds at lift stations and plants should check in with dispatch at set times, lock gates behind them and keep the radio on their belt, not in the truck.

**Public Services.** Flaggers should never step in front of a moving vehicle to stop it, and should radio the plate of anyone who runs the closure. Plow operators confronted over a plowed-in driveway should stay in the cab and keep moving. Forestry crews removing a parkway tree should expect a protest and call the supervisor rather than debate ownership. Facilities staff in public buildings should know the lockdown procedure and where the duress button is.

**Everyone.** Use the buddy system after dark and at flagged addresses. Keep your lone worker check-in times. Report broken lights, gates and locks as safety hazards. Know the radio **duress code** and use it early. When something feels wrong, leave; no shutoff, pickup or pothole is worth getting hurt over.

key_takeaways: Workplace violence includes threats, harassment and intimidation, not just physical assault, and it comes in four types: criminal intent, customer or public, worker on worker, and personal relationship.
Public works crews are exposed because they work in public and on private property, deliver unwelcome news like shutoffs and closures, and often work alone or at night.
Stay in 'yellow' all shift: know the normal baseline, find two exits, keep the phone away and trust your gut.

Warning signs such as escalating anger, threats, talk of weapons and fixation on a grievance call for a report to your supervisor, safety or human resources, not a diagnosis, and reporting is protected from retaliation.
With an angry resident or driver, stay calm, give space, listen, do not argue policy, offer the supervisor's number, never block an exit, and leave if it is not working.
In an active shooter event, Run if you can, Hide with the door locked, lights off and phone silenced if you cannot, and Fight with full commitment only as a last resort.
When police arrive, show empty hands with fingers spread, follow commands and do not stop officers for help; then go to the rally point so your supervisor can account for the crew.

questions.text: A resident shouts at a water technician that he will 'be waiting with his shotgun' the next time the truck comes down the street, but never leaves his porch. Under OSHA's definition, what is this?
options: Not workplace violence, because there was no physical contact
Workplace violence, because a threat of physical violence at the work site counts
A customer service complaint to be logged with billing
Workplace violence only if the resident has a criminal record
questions.explanation: OSHA's definition covers any act or threat of physical violence, harassment, intimidation or other threatening behavior at the work site. A spoken threat is workplace violence and must be reported, even with no contact.

questions.text: A plant operator's former partner, who has no connection to the department, shows up at the treatment plant gate demanding to see her. Which type of workplace violence is this?
options: Type 1, criminal intent
Type 2, customer or member of the public
Type 3, worker on worker
Type 4, personal relationship
questions.explanation: Type 4 is violence brought to work by someone with a personal relationship to the victim, usually a current or former partner. That is why employees are asked to tell a supervisor or human resources about protective orders and threats from an ex-partner.

questions.text: In the color code of awareness, which level should you be in for your whole shift?
options: Yellow: relaxed and alert, noticing who is around and where the exits are
White: focused on the task with everything else tuned out
Orange: focused on a specific person who may be a threat
Red: ready to leave or defend yourself at any second
questions.explanation: Yellow is the working state: relaxed, alert and aware of the baseline. White is switched off and belongs at home, while orange and red are responses to a specific concern or a confirmed threat.

questions.text: What do the letters in OODA stand for?
options: Open, organize, direct, alert
Observe, order, defend, alarm
Observe, orient, decide, act
Obey, obstruct, depart, assist
questions.explanation: OODA is observe, orient, decide, act: take in the scene, work out what it means, choose a response and carry it out, then look again. The habit of looking before acting is the point.

questions.text: A mechanic tells you his coworker has been talking for weeks about 'getting even' with the shop supervisor over a write-up and recently started bringing up the guns he owns. What should you do?
options: Keep an eye on him yourself and decide whether he is serious
Report what was said, as specifically as you can, to your supervisor, the safety office or human resources
Confront the coworker directly and tell him to stop talking like that
Wait until he makes a direct threat so the report will be taken seriously
questions.explanation: Fixation on a grievance and talk of weapons are warning signs. Your job is to report what you saw and heard, not to diagnose or confront. The threat assessment team decides what it means, and reporting in good faith is protected from retaliation.

questions.text: You are shutting off water for nonpayment and the homeowner comes out yelling and steps toward you. Which response follows the course?
options: Explain the shutoff policy in detail until he understands why he is wrong
Stand your ground between him and his front door so he cannot get closer
Tell him you will call the police if he says one more word
Keep your voice low, give him space, offer the supervisor's number, and leave if he does not calm down
questions.explanation: De-escalation means a calm voice, space, listening, not arguing policy and offering someone to call. Never block a person's exit, and if the person is not calming down, walk to the truck and leave. The shutoff can wait.

questions.text: You hear gunfire in the administration building and cannot reach an exit. What should you do?
options: Get into a room that locks, lock and barricade the door, turn off the lights and silence your phone completely
Lie down in the hallway and stay still so the shooter thinks you are already hurt
Set your phone to vibrate so you can still take calls from your supervisor
Leave the door unlocked so police can get in quickly
questions.explanation: When running is not possible, hide out of sight in a locked, barricaded room with the lights off and the phone fully silenced, including vibrate. Stay quiet and behind something solid until law enforcement says it is clear.

questions.text: Police enter the building while you are evacuating. What should you do?
options: Run to the nearest officer and hold on until you are escorted out
Stop the first officer you see and ask which way to go
Show empty hands with fingers spread, make no sudden movements, follow commands and keep moving in the direction the officers came from
Point toward the shooter and shout a description so officers hear you
questions.explanation: Officers' first job is to stop the shooter, and they do not know you from the attacker. Empty hands up, fingers spread, no sudden movements, follow commands and do not stop officers for help or directions.

questions.text: You have escaped to your truck and are calling 911. Which information does the dispatcher need most?
options: The location including building and floor, the number of shooters, their description, the weapons and how many people are hurt
Your employee number and your supervisor's name
The make and model of your truck and where it is parked
A list of coworkers you believe are still inside, with their phone numbers
questions.explanation: Dispatchers need the location, the number of shooters, what they look like, the kind of weapons and the number of people hurt. Accounting for coworkers happens at the rally point through your supervisor.

questions.text: Which practice is part of the department's approach to lone and night work at lift stations, substations and remote yards?
options: Turning off the radio at remote sites to avoid distraction
Leaving gates open so you can leave quickly if threatened
Working alone only during daylight hours, with no check-ins needed
Checking in with dispatch at set times, locking gates behind you and keeping the radio on your belt
questions.explanation: Lone worker check-ins at set times, locked gates, lighting and access control, and a radio within reach with a known duress code are the practices that protect people working alone or at night.
